data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The distinction between safe and idempotent in RFC 9110 is fundamentally about the presence of side effects: safe methods have none (they are read-only operations that do not modify any server resource), while idempotent methods may have side effects but guarantee that the side effects of repeated identical requests equal those of a single request. For an append-only event log, the required property is idempotence. The log cannot require safety because appending is inherently a mutation. But it must require idempotence because at-least-once delivery means the writer's append request may be received and processed multiple times, and the log must remain correct \u2014 containing each logical event exactly once regardless of how many times the delivery layer retries.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the event log tolerates duplicate events (e.g., consumers are designed to handle duplicates), then neither safety nor idempotence is strictly required of writers","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the at-least-once delivery layer provides its own deduplication before the log sees any retries, then the log writers need neither property","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Safe = no side effects (read-only). Idempotent = side effects allowed but invariant under repetition. At-least-once delivery means the network may deliver the same append request multiple times. If the append operation is not idempotent, each redelivery creates a new duplicate event, corrupting the log. If it is idempotent (via deduplication keys or sequence numbering), redelivery is absorbed as a no-op. Safety would be self-defeating: it would mean the append does nothing, making the log useless.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
